assumptions: The initial product targets one supplier type and a limited control framework.
Qualified security specialists review evidence rather than AI making unsupported assurance judgments.
Suppliers retain granular control over which evidence each buyer can access.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A paid supplier cohort and at least one anchor buyer accepting the standardized profile, measured reduction in questionnaire hours, repeat reuse across buyers, viable specialist-review margins, and credible security and liability controls.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: Reusable, permissioned evidence directly addresses duplicated supplier-assurance work intensified by supply-chain security obligations.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Repeated questionnaires and scarce security staff imply real labor burden, but neither supplier nor buyer willingness to fund a standardized exchange is validated.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Annual prepaid subscriptions could be attractive, but 15-50 hours of onboarding, specialist review, enterprise sales, security certification, liability, and two-sided support threaten margins and payback.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Polish SME suppliers serving affected enterprises are a definable niche, though applicability, questionnaire intensity, and addressable supplier counts require segmentation.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: Local language and SME specialization may win a niche, but established GRC and procurement platforms have buyer relationships, integrations, and trust advantages.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: Accepted profiles can expand across buyers, standards, tenders, continuous monitoring, remediation partners, insurance, and additional EU geographies.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: A trusted supplier-buyer network and reusable mappings can compound meaningfully, but only after achieving buyer acceptance; currently no data rights or network exists.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Evidence reuse can sharply reduce repeated work, yet buyers may still insist on proprietary questionnaires and fresh validation, limiting reuse value.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: NIS2 implementation guidance and heightened supply-chain scrutiny create a strong near-term adoption catalyst amid SME expertise constraints.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Cyber advisers and buyer invitations could scale efficiently, but the founder has no anchor buyer, supplier evidence, adviser commitment, or direct security-market access.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A narrow evidence pack is buildable, but secure custody, expert validation, breach exposure, enterprise trust, variable legal applicability, and marketplace liquidity are demanding for a part-time founder.

highest_value_structural_change: Start buyer-sponsored with one anchor enterprise that mandates or accepts a standardized evidence profile across its supplier cohort, solving distribution and evidence-acceptance simultaneously.
main_structural_strength: If buyer acceptance is achieved, each additional accepted supplier profile and mapping increases reusable network value and retention.
primary_score_limiter: The concept depends on two-sided adoption and trust, yet no anchor buyer accepts the evidence and acquisition economics are likely enterprise-heavy.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Entrenched GRC suites already serve major buyers, while legal applicability and acceptable evidence vary by buyer.
